title: How Clear Aligners Move Teeth: The Science Explained
metaTitle: How Clear Aligners Move Teeth: The Science
metaDescription: An evidence-informed look at how clear aligners move teeth: biomechanics, attachments, treatment staging and limitations for Ontario patients.
excerpt: An evidence-informed explanation of the biomechanics behind clear aligner therapy: how controlled forces, attachments and staged trays guide orthodontic tooth movement.

bodyHtml:
Introduction

Clear aligners have become one of the most recognizable developments in modern orthodontics, yet many people are surprised to learn that the gentle plastic trays they wear are capable of moving teeth through bone at all. Understanding how clear aligners move teeth requires looking past the appliance itself and into the biology of the tooth-supporting tissues. Teeth are not fused to the jaw; they are suspended in bone by a thin, living ligament that responds to sustained pressure in remarkable ways. When a sequence of precisely shaped aligners applies light, controlled forces, the supporting structures remodel, and teeth migrate toward their planned positions over weeks and months.

This article explains the clinical and biological science behind aligner therapy for dental professionals and informed patients alike. We will cover the biomechanics of tooth movement, the role of attachments and auxiliaries, how treatment is staged digitally, and the practical limitations and risks every patient should understand before beginning. For readers weighing their options more broadly, our overview of clear aligners versus fixed braces offers a useful companion read.

The Biology Behind Orthodontic Tooth Movement

All orthodontic tooth movement, whether driven by metal brackets or clear plastic, relies on the same underlying biology. The force applied by an appliance is transmitted to the periodontal ligament (PDL), the connective tissue that occupies the narrow space between the tooth root and the surrounding alveolar bone. This ligament is central to how teeth reposition.

The Periodontal Ligament and Bone Remodelling

When a sustained force pushes a tooth in a given direction, the PDL is compressed on one side of the root and stretched on the other. On the compression side, specialized cells called osteoclasts are recruited to resorb bone, effectively clearing a path for the tooth. On the tension side, osteoblasts lay down new bone to fill the widening space behind the moving root. This coordinated cycle of resorption and deposition is known as bone remodelling, and it is what allows a tooth to migrate through what otherwise appears to be solid jawbone.

Light, Continuous Force Versus Heavy Force

A key principle in orthodontics is that light, continuous forces tend to produce more efficient and biologically favourable tooth movement than heavy, intermittent ones. Excessive force can compress the PDL so severely that its blood supply is cut off, creating areas of tissue death that actually slow movement. Clear aligners are generally designed to deliver forces within a controlled range, and their staged nature means each tray introduces a small, incremental change rather than a large sudden one. This measured approach is one reason aligner therapy is often described as working through a series of gentle nudges rather than abrupt repositioning.

How the Aligner Itself Generates Force

A clear aligner is manufactured to a shape that differs slightly from the current position of the teeth. When the patient seats the tray, the plastic must flex to fit over teeth that are not yet where the aligner "expects" them to be. That stored elastic energy in the plastic is released as a continuous light pressure against specific tooth surfaces, and it is this pressure that drives movement toward the programmed position.

Sequential Trays and Incremental Movement

No single aligner attempts to achieve the full correction. Instead, a treatment plan is divided into a series of trays, each programmed to move targeted teeth a fraction of a millimetre or a few degrees of rotation. The patient wears each tray for a prescribed period, commonly one to two weeks, before advancing to the next in the sequence. Over the full series, these small increments accumulate into the final planned result. This is why consistent wear is so important: the biology needs sustained force over sufficient hours per day, and skipping or rushing trays can leave teeth lagging behind the plan.

The Importance of Wear Time

Because aligners are removable, their effectiveness depends heavily on patient compliance. Most clinicians recommend wearing trays for the great majority of each day, removing them primarily for eating, drinking anything other than water, and cleaning. Inadequate wear time interrupts the continuous force the biology requires, which can stall movement and extend overall treatment duration. This dependence on patient behaviour is one of the meaningful differences from fixed braces, which work continuously because they cannot be removed.

The Role of Attachments and Auxiliaries

Flat plastic pressing against a smooth, rounded tooth is well suited to some movements but poorly suited to others. To expand the range of achievable corrections, clinicians add small tooth-coloured composite shapes to selected teeth. These engineered features, along with other auxiliaries, are what allow aligners to perform more complex movements.

What Attachments Do

Attachments are precisely positioned bumps of bonded composite resin that give the aligner something to grip and push against. By creating a defined surface, they let the tray deliver forces in directions that would otherwise cause it to simply slip off the tooth, such as extrusion (pulling a tooth downward), rotation of a rounded tooth, or controlled tipping. Different attachment shapes are designed to encourage different force systems. Our detailed guide to clear aligner attachments explores these features and their clinical rationale in greater depth.

Other Auxiliaries

Beyond attachments, clinicians may use additional tools to achieve specific goals. Elastics anchored to buttons or precut notches can help correct how the upper and lower teeth meet. Interproximal reduction, the careful removal of tiny amounts of enamel between teeth, can create space for alignment in selected cases. These auxiliaries broaden the scope of what aligners can accomplish, though they also add complexity that benefits from careful planning and monitoring.

Digital Planning: From Scan to Tray

Modern aligner therapy is fundamentally a digital process. The accuracy of tooth movement depends not only on the appliance but on the quality of the plan that defines where each tooth should go and in what order.

Intraoral Scanning and Virtual Set-Up

Treatment usually begins with a digital impression captured by an intraoral scanner, which builds a precise three-dimensional model of the teeth and gums. From this model, the clinician and software construct a virtual treatment plan that stages the movement of each tooth from its starting position to its target. Readers interested in the underlying process can review our overview of aligner treatment planning.

Clinician Oversight of the Plan

While software can propose a sequence, the plan is a clinical document that should be reviewed and refined by the treating dentist or orthodontist. The practitioner evaluates whether the proposed movements are biologically realistic, whether anchorage is adequate, and where attachments or auxiliaries are needed. A visually appealing digital animation does not guarantee the same outcome in the mouth, and professional judgement remains essential to a sound plan.

Comparing Aligner Movements by Complexity

Not all tooth movements are equally predictable with aligners. The table below summarizes how different movement types generally relate to aligner biomechanics. It is intended as a broad clinical orientation, not a promise of results for any individual case.

Movement TypeRelative Predictability with AlignersTypical Supporting Features
Minor crowding or spacingOften well suitedSequential trays, sometimes interproximal reduction
Tipping of front teethGenerally favourableTray geometry alone or simple attachments
Rotation of rounded teethMore challengingOptimized attachments
Extrusion (pulling a tooth down)More challengingAttachments, sometimes auxiliaries
Bodily movement and bite changesCase dependent, often complexAttachments, elastics, careful anchorage planning

For a focused discussion of harder scenarios, see our article on complex orthodontic cases with clear aligners.

Clinical Limitations and Risks

Aligner therapy is a legitimate orthodontic modality, but it is not universally appropriate and it carries the same general risks as other forms of tooth movement. A candid understanding of these limitations supports realistic expectations.

Case Selection Matters

Some malocclusions, particularly those involving significant skeletal discrepancies or large bodily movements, may be less predictable with aligners alone and may be better addressed with fixed appliances or combined approaches. Thorough diagnosis, including appropriate records and imaging, helps determine suitability. The Canadian Dental Association and provincial bodies such as the Royal College of Dental Surgeons of Ontario emphasize diagnosis and professional supervision for any orthodontic treatment, which is why remote or unsupervised aligner arrangements raise concern among many clinicians.

Compliance and Biological Risks

Because results depend on consistent wear, inadequate compliance is a common reason treatment stalls or fails to reach its goal. Beyond compliance, orthodontic movement in general can be associated with risks such as root resorption, where root length is shortened, and gum recession when teeth are moved beyond their supporting bone. Pre-existing gum disease should be controlled before and monitored during treatment so that teeth are moved within healthy, supportive tissues. Mild discomfort and pressure when switching to a new tray are common and usually temporary.

Retention After Treatment

Teeth have a natural tendency to drift back toward their former positions once active movement stops, a phenomenon known as relapse. For this reason, retention is not optional; it is a permanent phase of orthodontic care. Patients typically wear retainers, often on a reducing schedule over time, to hold the result. Our article on orthodontic retention after clear aligners explains why this step is essential to protecting the outcome.

Frequently Asked Questions

How exactly do clear aligners move teeth?

Each aligner is shaped slightly differently from the current position of the teeth. When worn, the plastic flexes and releases a light, continuous force onto specific teeth. That force compresses the periodontal ligament on one side of the root and stretches it on the other, triggering bone to resorb ahead of the tooth and rebuild behind it. Over a series of trays, these small movements accumulate into the planned correction.

Do clear aligners hurt?

Many patients feel mild pressure, tightness, or tenderness for a day or two after switching to a new tray, which reflects the forces being applied to the teeth. This sensation usually eases as the tooth begins to respond. Persistent or severe pain is not expected and should be discussed with the treating clinician rather than ignored.

Why are small bumps bonded to my teeth during aligner treatment?

Those bumps are attachments, small pieces of tooth-coloured composite that give the aligner a defined surface to grip. They allow the tray to deliver forces for movements that would otherwise cause the plastic to slip, such as rotating rounded teeth or extruding a tooth. They are generally removed at the end of treatment.

Can clear aligners fix every orthodontic problem?

No. Aligners handle many cases well, but certain complex movements and significant skeletal discrepancies may be less predictable and sometimes better treated with fixed braces or combined approaches. A proper diagnosis by a qualified dentist or orthodontist determines whether aligners are an appropriate option for a given case.

What happens if I do not wear my aligners enough?

Aligners only work while they are in the mouth delivering force. Insufficient wear interrupts the continuous pressure the biology needs, which can slow or stall tooth movement and extend overall treatment time. Teeth may also fail to track with the planned sequence, sometimes requiring additional trays to recover.

Conclusion

Clear aligners move teeth by harnessing the same biological principles that underpin all orthodontics: sustained light force applied to the periodontal ligament, which prompts the surrounding bone to remodel and permits teeth to migrate into new positions. The appliance achieves this through precisely staged trays, often supported by attachments and auxiliaries, all guided by a carefully reviewed digital plan. Success depends heavily on consistent wear, sound case selection, and a committed retention phase to prevent relapse. For patients, the takeaway is that aligner therapy is a sophisticated, biologically grounded treatment that works best under professional supervision and with realistic expectations. Anyone considering it in Ontario should seek a thorough assessment from a qualified dental professional who can confirm suitability and tailor the plan to their individual needs.
